name: Snake
description: Pit organs detect temperature differences of 0.003C, creating thermal maps overlaid on visual input. Jacobson's organ analyzes air molecules via forked tongue stereoscopy. Four locomotion algorithms selected by terrain geometry.

core_attributes.neurology: pit organ IR neurons, Jacobson's organ chemosensory, multi-mode locomotion CPG
core_attributes.pattern: infrared thermal imaging, chemical stereoscopy, terrain-adaptive locomotion

scope.definition: Minimum detectable temperature differential of pit viper pit organ — smallest prey-background temperature difference (°C) eliciting directed strike behavior in controlled dark-room experiments.

evidence.source: Goris (2011) 'Infrared organs of snakes: an integral part of vision', Journal of Herpetology 45:2-14; Newman & Hartline (1982) 'The infrared vision of snakes', Scientific American 246:116-127.
cross_domain_examples: rattlesnake pit organ detects 0.003°C temperature differential — sensitivity exceeding most engineered IR sensors
pit membrane radiates >20 nm IR wavelengths with single-receptor quantum-limit sensitivity
FLIR thermal cameras: engineered equivalent achieves 0.050°C NETD — snake achieves 15× better

scope.falsifiability: If rattlesnakes fail to accurately strike at objects with temperature differentials below 0.03°C in complete darkness, the 0.003°C sensitivity claim overstates functional threshold.
scope.measurement_limits: Sensitivity measured for stationary warm objects against cool backgrounds. Moving prey detection threshold is higher (0.01-0.02°C). Resolution (spatial acuity) is poor — 1 pixel per degree.

scope.definition: Angular resolution of snake tongue-flicking chemical imaging — minimum angular separation of two odor sources distinguishable by bifurcated tongue-to-Jacobson's-organ signal comparison.

evidence.source: Schwenk (1994) 'Why snakes have forked tongues', Science 263:1573-1577; Kubie & Halpern (1975) forked tongue chemoreception studies.
cross_domain_examples: king snake resolves two scent trails 3 cm apart at 30 cm — 5.7° angular resolution
bifurcation creates stereo gradient comparison: same principle as binaural sound localization
crayfish paired antennules: convergent bilateral chemoreceptor stereo for plume source localization

scope.falsifiability: If snakes with surgically fused tongue tips show no impairment in trail-following accuracy compared to intact snakes, the bifurcated-tongue stereo hypothesis is unsupported.
scope.measurement_limits: Stereo resolution depends on inter-fork spacing relative to odor gradient width. Most effective in continuous odor trails; point-source localization in still air is more variable.

scope.definition: Fraction of terrestrial locomotion modes (lateral undulation, sidewinding, rectilinear, concertina) available to a generalist snake species on substrates ranging from loose sand to rough rock.

evidence.source: Jayne (1986) 'Kinematics of terrestrial snake locomotion', Copeia 1986:915-927; Gray (1953) 'Undulatory propulsion', Quarterly Journal of Microscopical Science 94:551-578.
cross_domain_examples: sidewinding rattlesnake: static friction approach achieving zero slippage on loose sand — engineered robots can't replicate fully
concertina mode in narrow tubes: 0.25× normal speed but 100% passage success in tunnel-width gaps
rectilinear locomotion via ventral scale ratcheting: the only undulatory locomotion mode without lateral body contact
snake robot locomotion: 4-mode switching replicating biological locomotion across 8 substrate types

scope.falsifiability: If a snake species is found that uses only one locomotion mode across all substrate types, the adaptive multi-mode model does not apply to that species.
scope.measurement_limits: Mode switching responsiveness varies by species. Highly specialized sidewinders (Crotalus cerastes) show poor performance in forest-litter concertina contexts. Generalist species (ratsnakes) show widest mode flexibility.
